sentences.text: The tower sequencing function translates the frozen operational targets from the regional flow process into an executable runway order for departures at Meridian Regional Airport.
In this section, Tower Sequence Manager is also called Ironleaf for tower sequencing discussions.
The Tower Supervisor is the operational owner of the departure sequence and uses the Tower Sequence Manager to confirm that each flight can be advanced without creating unsafe surface compression.
The workflow starts when the Flight Data Exchange provides current flight intent data and the Departure Metering Service aligns each Target Off Block Time with the applicable Calculated Takeoff Time.
The Tower Sequence Manager then builds a provisional order by runway, departure fix, aircraft wake category, and locally configured spacing rule.
The North Runway Meter and South Runway Meter maintain separate queues, but the Tower Supervisor can view both queues together when runway balancing is required.
The Surface Surveillance Adapter confirms whether an aircraft is still at stand, entering the movement area, holding short, or already committed to the departure stream.
The East Apron Sensor and West Apron Sensor improve queue accuracy by detecting aircraft movement before manual ramp status updates are available.
The Ramp Control Lead coordinates pushback release priorities against stand conflicts, taxi lane constraints, and the runway demand visible in the Tower Sequence Manager.
The Airline Operations Coordinator may request a sequence review when a flight has a valid operational reason to protect a connection, crew limit, or network rotation.
The Slot Coordinator verifies that any proposed resequencing remains compatible with the Calculated Takeoff Time tolerance and the current Slot Compliance State.
The Regional Flow Manager is notified when local resequencing threatens to erode the planned departure rate in the Airport Capacity Plan.
Runway queue management favors stable ordering, but the Tower Supervisor may intervene when wake spacing, route restrictions, runway crossings, or emergency traffic require a change.
Each manual sequence change is recorded in the Collaborative Decision Log with the user identity, timestamp, affected flight, and reason code.
The Audit Event Ledger preserves the sequence history so that post-event review can distinguish operational necessity from avoidable volatility.
Departure readiness checks combine aircraft operator status, ground handling status, cockpit readiness, route clearance availability, and surface position into a single tower-readable indicator.
The Aircraft Operator Representative is responsible for keeping aircraft readiness information current enough for the tower team to trust the displayed status.
The Ground Handling Dispatcher updates boarding, loading, door closure, and tow readiness milestones through the operational interface before the flight is considered eligible for pushback planning.
Foxglove shall publish tower readiness changes to authenticated airline and handling users within the configured refresh interval.
The Deicing Coordinator sends the Deicing Pad Queue Card when pad demand, treatment progress, or release timing changes.
The deicing interface point exposes whether a flight still requires treatment, is waiting for pad access, is under treatment, or has been released for taxi within the protected time assumption.
When deicing demand increases, the Tower Supervisor compares pad release expectations with runway queue gaps before accepting an aircraft into the active departure stream.

During Adverse Weather Mode or a Capacity Reduction State, the Tower Sequence Manager applies the active spacing rules from the Business Rules Registry and highlights flights that may miss their Calculated Takeoff Time.
In the Recovery Phase, the tower sequence workflow emphasizes measured acceleration rather than first-come recovery, because uncontrolled pushback surges can overload taxiways and recreate delay.
